a: climbed the mountain
p: Matthew sets the first great sermon on a mountain, as Moses received the Law on Sinai.
b: Matthew gives no name for the mountain; the Greek has "the mountain," perhaps meaning the hill country above the lake. Readers who knew the Torah heard an echo: "Moses climbed up to God" (Exodus 19:3), and "I had gone up the mountain to receive the stone tablets" (Deuteronomy 9:9). Jesus now goes up and gives his own teaching on the Law (5:17–48). Many scholars see this as part of Matthew's picture of Jesus as a new Moses (2:13–21; 4:2). Others warn not to press it: Jesus does not bring tablets down, and Matthew often puts Jesus on mountains (14:23; 15:29; 17:1; 28:16). Luke places a shorter form of the sermon on "a level place" (Luke 6:17). Since the 300s, pilgrims have remembered the spot on the hills above Capernaum, the "Mount of Beatitudes."

a: Once he was seated
p: Jewish teachers sat to teach, as Jesus does here and in the synagogue at Nazareth.
b: Sitting was the posture of a teacher with authority. Jesus sits to read and explain in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4:20), sits in the Temple courts to teach (26:55), and speaks of the scribes who "sit on Moses' seat" (23:2). Students stood or sat at the teacher's feet (Luke 10:39; Acts 22:3). The disciples "came to him" as students to a master, while the crowds listen from around them (7:28).

a: he opened his mouth to teach them
p: A solemn Hebrew way of saying that someone begins an important speech.
b: The Greek, "opening his mouth he taught them," copies a Hebrew way of marking a weighty speech (Job 3:1; Daniel 10:16; Acts 8:35; 10:34). Matthew uses it once, here, at the start of the first of the five long teachings in his Gospel. "Taught" is in the Greek imperfect, which can mean "began to teach" or "went on teaching."
orig: ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ ἐδίδασκεν (anoixas to stoma autou edidasken)

a: Blessed
p: Makarios announces that someone is already well off in God's eyes. It is not "may you be blessed."
b: The Greek makarios stands for Hebrew ashrei, the first word of the Psalms: "Happy is the person" (Psalm 1:1). It is a statement, not a prayer: it congratulates someone. Some versions say "Happy," which catches the joy but can sound like a passing mood. "Blessed" keeps the sense that God is the one who makes them well off, though it is not the word for "bless" (eulogeō). These sayings are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus. The surprise is who is congratulated: the poor, the grieving, the hungry, the persecuted. Luke's version has four blessings and four woes (Luke 6:20–26).

a: poor in spirit
p: Not lacking in spirit, but the humble poor who know they need God, as in Isaiah 61.
b: Luke has "you who are poor" (Luke 6:20); Matthew adds "in spirit." The phrase does not mean timid or spiritually empty. In the Hebrew Bible "the poor" ('aniyyim, 'anawim) are often the humble who depend on God because they have no other help (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1). The Dead Sea Scrolls use almost the same words, "the poor in spirit" (War Scroll 14:7), for the faithful remnant. Most interpreters take Matthew's phrase as humility before God, joined to real need. Others, reading with Luke, stress actual poverty and see "in spirit" as describing the attitude, not replacing the condition. The blessings of 5:3–5 follow Isaiah 61:1–3 closely: good news to the poor, comfort for mourners, an inheritance in the land.
orig: οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι (hoi ptōchoi tō pneumati)

a: they will be comforted
p: The passive verbs in the Beatitudes mean that God will comfort, fill and show mercy.
b: "They will be comforted," "they will be given their fill," "mercy will be shown to them," "they will be called sons of God": Jewish speech often used the passive to speak of God's acts without naming him, and the Plain keeps the passive. The mourners are those who grieve over their own losses and over the state of God's people, as in Isaiah 61:2–3, where the anointed messenger comes "to comfort all who mourn" in Zion. The comfort is the coming of God's kingdom.

a: the gentle
p: This blessing quotes Psalm 37:11 in its Greek form. "Meek" here means gentle, not weak.
b: The line comes from Psalm 37:11, which the site's Plain renders "But the humble will take possession of the land / and delight in great peace." The Greek Psalm uses the same words Matthew does: hoi praeis klēronomēsousin gēn. In the Psalm the 'anawim are the humble poor who wait for God instead of grabbing land by force; the land is Israel's land. Matthew's gē can mean "land" or "earth," and the promise has been read both ways: the land of Israel renewed, or the whole earth made new (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1). Praus is not weakness. Matthew uses it of Jesus himself, "I am gentle and my heart is humble" (11:29), and of the king who comes on a donkey (21:5). The older English "meek" meant mild and patient.

a: hungry and thirsty for righteousness
p: Righteousness can mean a right life before God, or God setting the world right. Both may be meant.
b: Dikaiosynē is a key word in Matthew (3:15; 5:10, 20; 6:1, 33; 21:32). Here it can mean the right conduct God asks for, so the blessed long to live as God wants. It can also mean justice: God setting things right for the oppressed, which Luke's version suggests: "you who are hungry now" (Luke 6:21). Many readers take Matthew to mean both: those who ache for God's will to be done in themselves and in the world (6:10). The image of hunger and thirst for God goes back to the Psalms and the prophets (Psalm 42:2; Isaiah 55:1–2), and the promise of being fed full recalls the feast of the age to come (Isaiah 25:6).
orig: πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην (peinōntes kai dipsōntes tēn dikaiosynēn)

a: Blessed are the merciful
p: The merciful will be shown mercy: a theme that runs through Matthew and through Jewish teaching.
b: This blessing has the same shape as "the measure you use" (7:2) and "forgive us ... as we ... have forgiven" (6:12). Matthew twice has Jesus quote Hosea 6:6, "I want mercy, not sacrifice" (9:13; 12:7), and his parable of the unforgiving slave ends with a man who received mercy and showed none (18:23–35). Jewish teachers said the same: "Whoever has mercy on people, heaven has mercy on him" is a saying in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 151b). Proverbs gives the earlier form: "happy is the one who is kind to the lowly" (Proverbs 14:21).

a: those whose hearts are pure
t: Pure in heart, they will see God
p: This blessing echoes Psalm 24: the one with a pure heart may climb the LORD's mountain.
b: Psalm 24 asks, "Who can climb the LORD's mountain?" and answers, "Someone whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure" (Psalm 24:3–4). In the Bible the heart is the center of thought and will, not only feelings, so a pure heart is an undivided one: no double life, no hidden aims (6:22–24; 15:18–19). "Seeing God" was the hope of worshipers in the Temple (Psalm 42:2) and the promise of the end (Revelation 22:4). Yet Scripture also says no one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20). Christian writers have read this verse as the promise of the "beatific vision," seeing God face to face in the age to come (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2).
r: Psalm 24:3–4; Psalm 51:10; Exodus 33:20; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4

a: they will be called sons of God
p: Peacemakers will be called God's sons because they act like their Father. The Greek says "sons."
b: The Greek is huioi theou, "sons of God." Many modern versions say "children" because women are clearly included; the Plain keeps "sons" because in the Bible a son shares his father's character and inherits from him, and Paul writes, "you are all sons of God" to men and women alike (Galatians 3:26–28). Israel was God's son (Exodus 4:22), and here the title goes to those who make peace, as God does (5:45). In Matthew's world, the Roman emperor was hailed as the bringer of peace and as a son of a god. Jesus gives both names to people who reconcile enemies.

a: because the kingdom of heaven is theirs
p: The first and eighth blessings end with the same words, framing the set. The ninth turns to "you."
b: "Because the kingdom of heaven is theirs" ends both 5:3 and 5:10, so the eight blessings form one unit, and the present tense ("is") frames the six future promises between them. The first four blessings touch need (poor, grieving, gentle, hungry); the next four touch conduct (mercy, purity, peacemaking, faithfulness under pressure). Both sets end with "righteousness" (5:6, 10). Then 5:11 switches from "those" to "you," applying the last blessing to the disciples who are listening. Readers differ on whether the Beatitudes are entrance requirements (be like this and you will enter) or announcements of grace (God's kingdom comes to people like this). Many see both: they describe the people God welcomes and the people he is forming.

a: on account of me
p: The prophets suffered for God. Here Jesus says his followers will suffer for his sake.
b: In 5:10 the persecution is "on account of righteousness"; in 5:11 it is "on account of me." Jesus puts loyalty to himself where loyalty to God's ways stood, and compares his followers to the prophets (5:12). Many readers see a high claim about Jesus here. For Matthew's first readers, who were expelled from synagogues and harassed (10:17–23; 23:34), the blessing explained their suffering as a mark of belonging to Jesus.

a: People persecuted the prophets who lived before you
p: Elijah, Zechariah, Jeremiah and others suffered for speaking God's word. Jesus returns to this in 23:29–37.
b: Elijah complained, "They have killed your prophets with the sword" (1 Kings 19:10). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the Temple courtyard (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), Uriah was killed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20–23), and Jeremiah himself was beaten and jailed (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15). Later Jewish writings told of more martyred prophets, such as Isaiah sawn in two (Hebrews 11:37 may allude to it). Jesus returns to this theme in his sharpest speech (23:29–37). The disciples are placed in the line of the prophets: their suffering is not a sign that God has left them.
r: 1 Kings 19:10; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Nehemiah 9:26; 23:29–37; Hebrews 11:36–38; Acts 7:52

a: if salt goes flat
p: The Greek verb means "become foolish." Salt cannot lose its taste, but salt mixed with dirt could.
b: The verb mōrainō means "to make or become foolish" (Romans 1:22; 1 Corinthians 1:20), from mōros, "fool." Used of salt it means "to go tasteless," and the play on words may come from Aramaic, where tapel means both "tasteless" and "foolish." Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But the salt people gathered by the Dead Sea was mixed with other minerals; when the true salt was washed out, a flat white crust was left. Salt seasoned food, preserved it, and was part of every offering (Leviticus 2:13); a "covenant of salt" was one that lasted (Numbers 18:19). Disciples who lose what makes them different are useless. Mark and Luke have the saying in other settings (Mark 9:50; Luke 14:34–35).

a: You are the light of the world
t: Israel's calling, given to the disciples
p: Isaiah calls God's servant "a light to the nations." Jesus gives that role to his followers.
b: Isaiah says God's servant will be "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6), and pictures the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD's house (Isaiah 2:2–3) and coming to Jerusalem's light (Isaiah 60:1–3). Jewish writers called Israel, the Law and Jerusalem the light of the world. Jesus says it of a small group of Galilean disciples. In John's Gospel Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). "A city that stands on a mountain" may point to Jerusalem on Mount Zion, or simply to the hilltop towns any Galilean could see from far off; the popular idea that Jesus pointed to Sepphoris or Hippos is a guess.
r: Isaiah 2:2–3; Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 60:1–3; John 8:12; Philippians 2:15; 4:16

a: a grain basket
p: A small clay lamp lit a one-room house. The basket was a grain measure that could smother it.
b: Ordinary houses in Galilee had one main room, lit by a small clay oil lamp set on a stand or a ledge. The modios was a measuring container for grain, holding about two gallons. Putting it over the lamp would put the lamp out. Jesus' point is the absurdity: no one lights a lamp to hide it. Mark and Luke use the saying about the word of God (Mark 4:21; Luke 8:16); Matthew uses it about the disciples' visible lives.

a: give glory to your Father who is in heaven
t: Good works that point to God
p: The good deeds are to be seen, but the glory goes to the Father, not to the doer.
b: This seems to clash with 6:1–18, where good deeds must be hidden. The difference is the aim: here, people see the works and praise God; in 6:1, people do them "so that they will watch you." "Your Father" appears here for the first time in Matthew, and it returns again and again in the sermon. The Jewish idea of kiddush hashem, making God's name holy by one's conduct before others, is close to this verse (compare 6:9).

a: to fulfill them
p: Jesus did not come to scrap the Law and the Prophets. How he "fulfills" them is debated.
b: Plēroō means "to fill, to complete." Matthew uses it for prophecy coming true (1:22; 2:15). Readers have taken it in several ways: (1) Jesus obeys the Law perfectly; (2) he teaches its full and true meaning, as in 5:21–48; (3) he brings to pass what the Law and Prophets pointed to, so that they are fulfilled in him; (4) he "establishes" or upholds them, a sense the Aramaic qayyem could carry. Many combine (2) and (3). "The Law and the Prophets" means the Scriptures as a whole, and the same phrase closes the main body of the sermon (7:12). The Babylonian Talmud tells of a judge who quoted a saying from the "Gospel": "I did not come to take away from the Law of Moses, nor to add to it" (Shabbat 116b), a garbled echo of this verse.
orig: οὐκ ἦλθον καταλῦσαι ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι (ouk ēlthon katalysai alla plērōsai)

a: not one iota or one tiny hook of a letter
t: The smallest letter and its tiny hook
p: The iota stands for Hebrew yod, the smallest letter. The "hook" is a stroke that tells two letters apart.
b: The Greek iōta stands for the Hebrew letter yod (י), the smallest in the alphabet. The keraia, "little horn," is the tiny stroke that marks one Hebrew letter off from a similar one, such as ד (d) from ר (r), or a decorative stroke on a letter. The KJV's "jot and tittle" gave English an idiom. The point is that the Law stands down to its smallest detail. The verse has two "until" clauses: "until heaven and earth pass away" and "until all things have come about." Some read the second as the end of the age; others as the events of Jesus' death and resurrection, which bring the Law to its goal (28:18–20). Luke has a shorter form (Luke 16:17).
orig: ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία (iōta hen ē mia keraia)

a: Amen, I tell you
p: People said "amen" to agree with someone else's words. Jesus puts it first, to guarantee his own.
b: Amen is a Hebrew word meaning "surely, so be it." In the Hebrew Bible and in Jewish prayer it answers another person's prayer, blessing or curse (Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus turns it around: he says "Amen" before his own words, staking his authority on what follows. Matthew has the phrase more than thirty times, the first here; John doubles it ("Amen, amen"). Joachim Jeremias argued that no one before Jesus spoke this way; a Hebrew letter on a potsherd from about 600 BC (Yavneh-Yam) has a similar "amen" before a statement, so the use may not be entirely new, but it is a mark of Jesus' speech in all four Gospels. Many Bibles translate it "truly" or "I tell you the truth."
orig: ἀμὴν γὰρ λέγω ὑμῖν (amēn gar legō hymin)

a: will be called least in the kingdom of heaven
p: Which commands are meant, and does "least" mean shut out or simply low in rank?
b: "These commands" most naturally means the commands of the Law just mentioned (5:18). Some readers think it means Jesus' own commands in the sermon. Jewish teachers distinguished "light" and "heavy" commands but warned against neglecting the light ones (Mishnah Avot 2:1). "Called least in the kingdom" seems to mean a low place within it, not exclusion, which comes in 5:20. Critical scholars often hear here a Jewish-Christian community that kept the Law, and some (such as Betz) see a jab at Christians who taught that the Law no longer applied. Others reply that Matthew's Jesus reorders the Law's priorities (15:11; 23:23) and that "keep" means keep as Jesus interprets it. Matthew, unlike Mark 7:19, does not say that Jesus declared all foods clean.

a: overflow far beyond the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees
p: Not more rules, but a deeper obedience from the heart. The Pharisees were respected teachers of the Law.
b: The scribes were experts in the Law, and the Pharisees were a lay movement known for careful keeping of it. The people admired them (Josephus, Antiquities 18.15). So this saying would have shocked its hearers. The next verses show what "more" means: not adding rules, but obedience that reaches anger, desire, words and love for enemies (5:21–48), done for God and not for show (6:1–18). Matthew's sharp picture of the Pharisees reflects the conflict between his community and the synagogue leaders of his own day (23:1–36). Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine point out that the Pharisees' own teaching often matched what Jesus asks here, and that reading the verse as "Jews were legalists" is a caricature.

a: You have heard what the people of long ago were told
t: "You have heard ... but I myself tell you"
p: Six times Jesus quotes the Law, then says "But I myself tell you." Does he oppose the Law or deepen it?
b: These six sayings (5:21–48) are often called the antitheses. "The people of long ago" means the generation at Sinai; the Greek dative can also mean "by" them (KJV "by them of old time"), but most take it as "to." "You have heard" points to the Law as heard read aloud in the synagogue. Most readers think that in the first two (murder, adultery) Jesus deepens the command, reaching the heart. In the others (divorce, oaths, revenge, hatred) he seems to go beyond or even set aside what the Law allowed. Many scholars say none of them contradicts the Law: avoiding oaths keeps you from false oaths, and not divorcing keeps you from misusing divorce. Jewish teachers called this "making a fence around the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 1:1).

a: 'Whoever murders must stand trial.'
p: "Whoever murders must stand trial" is not a verse of the Law, but a summary of what it requires.
b: "You must not murder" is the sixth commandment as numbered by most Protestants and the Orthodox (Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17). The second line is not a quotation but sums up laws such as "Whoever hits someone and he dies must be put to death" (Exodus 21:12) and the rule that a killer must first stand trial in front of the community (Numbers 35:12). Krisis, "judgment," here means a local court of judges (Deuteronomy 16:18).
r: Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17; Exodus 21:12; Numbers 35:12; Deuteronomy 16:18; Genesis 9:6

a: But I myself tell you
p: Jesus does not cite other teachers. He sets his own word beside the words given at Sinai.
b: The Greek egō de legō hymin includes the pronoun "I," which Greek does not need, so it is emphatic. Teachers of the Law usually supported a ruling by citing earlier authorities or a verse. Jesus speaks on his own authority, which is what astonishes the crowds at the end (7:28–29). David Daube and Morton Smith showed that rabbis also used "but I say" in debate, setting their own view against another reading; the difference here is that Jesus sets his word beside the command of God itself.
orig: ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν (egō de legō hymin)

a: is angry with his brother
p: "Brother" means a fellow member of God's people. Later copies add "without cause."
b: "Brother" in Matthew means a fellow believer or fellow Israelite, man or woman (12:50; 18:15, 21; 23:8). The present tense suggests anger kept up, not a flash of temper. Many later manuscripts add eikē, "without a cause," which the KJV follows; see the variant at this phrase. Jesus himself shows anger in Matthew (21:12–13; 23), which is one reason copyists softened the saying. Jewish moral teaching also warned against nursing anger (Leviticus 19:17–18; Sirach 27:30).
orig: ὁ ὀργιζόμενος τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ (ho orgizomenos tō adelphō autou)

a: 'Raca,'
p: Raca is Aramaic for "empty head." The three penalties rise from a local court to the high council to Gehenna.
b: Rhaka is the Aramaic reqa, "empty one," a common insult. Mōre, "fool, idiot," is its Greek match. The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest. The three steps (local court, high court, fire of Gehenna) sound like a legal scale, but no court tried people for name-calling. Most scholars read the passage as deliberate exaggeration: Jesus mimics legal language to show that contempt is as serious before God as murder is in court. Some see real Jewish-Christian church discipline behind it. Matthew's Jesus calls people "blind fools" himself (23:17), which shows the warning is about contempt for a brother, not about every sharp word.

a: the fire of Gehenna
p: Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, a place of child sacrifice that became a name for final judgment.
b: Geenna is the Greek form of Hebrew ge-hinnom, "Valley of Hinnom," the ravine on the south side of Jerusalem (Joshua 15:8). Kings of Judah burned children there to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), and Jeremiah said it would become the "Valley of Slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:32). By Jesus' time Jewish writings used it as the name of the place where the wicked are punished by fire (1 Enoch 27:1–3; 4 Ezra 7:36). Most English versions translate it "hell," which hides the place name and mixes it with Hades, the realm of the dead. The common claim that the valley was a burning city rubbish dump is not attested in ancient sources or by excavation; the earliest known source is a comment by David Kimhi (about 1200) on Psalm 27:13. Matthew uses the word seven times (5:22, 29–30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:15, 33).
orig: τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρός (tēn geennan tou pyros)

a: presenting your offering at the altar
p: Jesus pictures a worshiper at the Temple altar. Making peace with a brother comes before the offering.
b: The scene is the Temple in Jerusalem, where offerings were handed to the priests at the great altar in the inner court. A Galilean might have walked three days to get there, so leaving the offering to go home and make peace is a vivid exaggeration. The teaching matches Jewish practice: "For sins between a person and his fellow, the Day of Atonement does not atone until he has made peace with his fellow" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). The prophets had long said that worship without right dealing is empty (Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24). Matthew's readers, after the Temple fell in AD 70, applied it to prayer and the Lord's Supper (Didache 14:2).

a: the man who is suing you
p: The picture is a debtor dragged to court and jailed until paid. Luke has it in a warning about judgment.
b: Antidikos is the other party in a lawsuit. The scene fits Roman and Hellenistic practice more than the Torah, which did not use prison for debt: a creditor could have a debtor jailed until his family paid (compare 18:30). The "guard" (hypēretēs) was the court officer who carried out the sentence. In Matthew the saying follows the teaching on reconciliation, so it is practical advice: settle quickly. In Luke it follows a warning to read the signs of the times, so it is about meeting God's judgment (Luke 12:57–59). Many readers hear both levels in Matthew too.

a: so as to lust after her
p: The Greek verb is the one used in the command "You must not crave your neighbor's wife."
b: In the Law, adultery meant a man having sex with another man's wife (Leviticus 20:10), and gynē can mean "woman" or "wife." The verb epithymeō, "to desire, crave," is the word of the Greek tenth commandment: "You must not crave your neighbor's wife" (Exodus 20:17). So Jesus joins the seventh and tenth commandments. Pros to epithymēsai means "for the purpose of desiring": not noticing someone, but looking in order to want her. Job had said, "I cut a covenant with my eyes" (Job 31:1), and Sirach 9:8 warns a man to turn his eyes from another man's wife. The saying puts the responsibility on the man who looks, not on the woman.
orig: πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn)
r: Exodus 20:14; Exodus 20:17; Job 31:1; Proverbs 6:25; 2 Samuel 11:2; James 1:14–15

a: pull it out and fling it away from you
p: Nearly all readers take this as deliberate exaggeration, though a few in history took it literally.
b: Jesus uses shocking images to make a point: nothing is worth losing yourself over, so deal ruthlessly with what leads you into sin. The "right" eye and hand were the more valued ones. Matthew repeats the saying in 18:8–9 about causing others to stumble, and Mark has a fuller form (Mark 9:43–48). Skandalizō, "trip up," means to make someone fall into sin, not just to offend. Eusebius reports that the young Origen castrated himself, taking a related saying (19:12) literally (Church History 6.8); in his later Commentary on Matthew (15.1–3) Origen rejects a literal reading of that verse; the church's Council of Nicaea (AD 325) barred self-castrated men from the clergy. Christians and Jews have understood such sayings as calls to self-discipline, not to self-harm.

a: a certificate of divorce
p: The Law required a husband to give his wife a written document. It set her free to remarry.
b: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 assumes a man may divorce his wife if "he has found something indecent in her" and requires him to write "a certificate of divorce" and put it in her hand. The law's main rule is that he cannot take her back after she has married another man. The written document, later called a get, protected the woman: it proved she was free. The Mishnah says its essential words are "You are permitted to any man" (Mishnah Gittin 9:3). Only the husband could issue it. Jesus quotes the requirement in shortened form; in 19:7–8 he says Moses permitted divorce because of hard hearts.

a: except sexual sin
p: Only Matthew has an exception. Its meaning, and whether it allows remarriage, divides the churches.
b: Mark 10:11–12, Luke 16:18 and Paul (1 Corinthians 7:10–11) give Jesus' teaching with no exception; Matthew has one here and in 19:9. Porneia is a broad word for sexual sin. Readings: (1) adultery or other sexual unfaithfulness, which gives the wronged husband grounds to divorce (most Protestants); (2) a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship (Leviticus 18; Acts 15:20), which was never valid, close to the Catholic idea of annulment; (3) unfaithfulness during betrothal, as Joseph suspected of Mary (1:18–19); (4) the exception allows a man to separate from an unfaithful wife, but not to remarry while she lives. This was the view of Jerome and Augustine, the Western church's reading for its first 1,500 years, defended by the Council of Trent and held by some evangelical scholars. The Orthodox churches allow divorce for adultery and, by pastoral "economy," a second marriage. The background is a Jewish debate: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for "a matter of indecency," the school of Hillel "even if she spoiled his dish" (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Jesus sides with the stricter view and goes further. See the card on this chapter's page.

a: he makes her an adulteress
t: Why would she become an adulteress?
p: In that world a divorced woman nearly always remarried. Jesus says the husband who sent her away shares the blame.
b: The Greek verb is passive, literally "he causes her to be adulterated." A divorced woman with no family support would almost certainly marry again. Jesus treats the first marriage as still binding before God, so her second marriage counts as adultery, and the husband who divorced her without cause is responsible for it. Some readers hear the passive as "makes her a victim of adultery": she is wronged, not guilty. The final clause ("if a man marries ...") is missing in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies.

a: you must pay to the Lord what you promised under oath
p: The quotation sums up several laws: do not swear falsely by God's name, and keep the vows you make.
b: No single verse says this. The first half recalls "Do not swear by my name to a lie" (Leviticus 19:12); the second, "When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to pay it" (Deuteronomy 23:21) and "he may not go back on his word" (Numbers 30:2). An oath called God as witness to the truth of a statement; a vow promised God something. The Law allowed and even commanded swearing by God's name (Deuteronomy 6:13). Here, as in all quotations of the Law, the Greek has kyrios, "Lord," where the Hebrew has the divine name YHWH.
r: Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Deuteronomy 6:13; Exodus 20:7; Zechariah 8:17

a: do not take oaths at all
p: People swore by heaven or Jerusalem to avoid God's name. Jesus says every oath still involves God.
b: To avoid using God's name, people swore by substitutes: heaven, earth, the Temple, the altar, Jerusalem, their own head. Some teachers debated which oaths were binding (the Mishnah lists oaths "by heaven and earth" that do not bind, Shevuot 4:13; and vows "as Jerusalem," Nedarim 1:3). Jesus attacks the same games in 23:16–22. Every one of these things belongs to God, so every oath involves him. The Essenes, Josephus says, avoided oaths and held them "worse than perjury" (Jewish War 2.135), and Sirach warns against the habit of swearing (Sirach 23:9–11). James 5:12 repeats this teaching. Paul calls God as witness in his letters (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), which is one reason many churches allow oaths in court.

a: the stool for his feet
p: These words come from Isaiah 66:1 and Psalm 48:2: heaven is God's throne, Jerusalem the great King's city.
b: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet" is God's word in Isaiah 66:1, quoted again by Stephen (Acts 7:49). Psalm 48:2 calls Mount Zion "the town of the great King"; Matthew's Greek has "city." Swearing by Jerusalem meant swearing by the place God chose for his name. Jesus' point: you cannot step outside God's world to make a promise that does not involve him.

a: say 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no.'
p: The doubled yes may itself be a firm form of affirmation. "The evil one" can also be read "evil."
b: The Greek repeats each word: "Yes, yes; no, no." It can mean "let your yes be a plain yes," as James 5:12 puts it, or the doubling may itself be a solemn affirmation instead of an oath. The Babylonian Talmud records the view that a doubled "yes" or "no" counts as an oath (Shevuot 36a). Ek tou ponērou can be "from the evil one" (masculine) or "from evil" (neuter). Matthew uses ho ponēros for the devil in 13:19 and 13:38, so the Plain has "the evil one" here and in 6:13. The meaning: the need for oaths comes from a world where lying is normal.
orig: ναὶ ναί, οὒ οὔ ... ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ (nai nai, ou ou ... ek tou ponērou)

a: 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.'
t: Eye for eye: a limit, not a license
p: The law of equal payback was meant for judges, to stop revenge from growing. It was never a rule for personal vengeance.
b: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth" appears three times in the Law (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It set the penalty a court could impose: no more than the harm done. Similar rules appear in the Code of Hammurabi. In Jesus' time Josephus says the injured person could accept money instead (Antiquities 4.280), and the later rabbis ruled that it always meant payment of money (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1). Jesus does not argue with the court rule; he speaks to the victim's urge to get even. Proverbs had already said, "Do not say, 'I will get even for the evil'" (Proverbs 20:22).
r: Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21; Proverbs 20:22; Proverbs 24:29; Romans 12:17–19

a: do not set yourself against the evil person
p: The Greek can mean "do not fight back," or "do not take legal action," or "do not resist violently."
b: Antistēnai means "to stand against, oppose," and was used of armed resistance and of opposing someone in court. Tō ponērō could be "evil" in general (KJV "resist not evil") but the examples that follow show a person: the one who slaps, sues and drafts you. The traditional reading: do not retaliate in personal matters; this does not abolish courts or governments (Romans 13:4). The Anabaptist and Quaker reading: Christians must not use force against anyone. Walter Wink and others argue that Jesus forbids violent resistance but teaches bold, nonviolent ways to resist humiliation. Jesus himself was struck and did not hit back (26:67), but he did protest (John 18:23). See the card on this page.
orig: μὴ ἀντιστῆναι τῷ πονηρῷ (mē antistēnai tō ponērō)

a: slaps your right cheek
t: A slap on the right cheek
p: For a right-handed person, hitting the right cheek means a backhand: an insult more than an injury.
b: A right-handed blow to someone's right cheek is a backhanded slap, which in that culture was a deliberate insult. The Mishnah fines a slap with the back of the hand at twice the rate of an ordinary slap (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:6). So the first example is about honor: do not answer an insult with an insult. The servant in Isaiah says, "My back I gave to the floggers ... I did not cover my face against insult and spit" (Isaiah 50:6), and Lamentations 3:30 speaks of offering the cheek to the one who strikes. Matthew alone says "right" cheek; Luke has simply "the cheek" (Luke 6:29).

a: the tunic you wear, give up your outer robe
p: The tunic was the inner garment; the outer robe was the one the Law said must be given back by night.
b: The chitōn was a long shirt worn next to the skin; the himation was the heavy outer robe that also served as a blanket. The Law protected a poor man's outer robe: "give it back to him by sundown, because it is his only covering" (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13). So a court could take the tunic as a pledge, but not hold the robe overnight. Jesus tells his hearers to give up even what the Law would let them keep. In Luke the order is reversed (Luke 6:29), which suggests a robbery instead of a lawsuit.

a: drafts you into service for one mile
t: Forced to carry for a mile
p: Soldiers and officials could force civilians to carry their gear. A Roman mile was about 1,000 paces.
b: Angareuō is a Persian loanword for the royal courier service, which could take people and animals to carry the king's post. Under Rome, soldiers and officials could compel civilians to carry baggage or provide animals, and there were rules to limit it. Matthew uses the same verb when the soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross (27:32). The "mile" (milion) was the Roman mile of a thousand double paces, about 1,480 meters. Jesus' hearers in occupied Galilee knew the resentment such orders caused. Going a second mile turns a forced task into a free gift.

a: If someone wants to borrow from you
p: The Law told Israelites to lend freely to a brother in need, even when the year of release was near.
b: Deuteronomy commands, "Open your hand wide to him, and lend him enough for whatever he lacks" (Deuteronomy 15:8), and warns against refusing because the seventh year, when debts were released, is near (Deuteronomy 15:9). The Law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite in need (Exodus 22:25). Jesus extends the generosity: not only to brothers, and without calculating. Luke adds "do not ask for it back" (Luke 6:30, 35).

a: and hate your enemy
t: "Hate your enemy" is not in the Law
p: The Law says "love your neighbor." No verse says "hate your enemy." Where does it come from?
b: Leviticus 19:18 says, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself." The words "and hate your enemy" are not in the Hebrew Bible, and Jesus does not say they are; he says "you have heard." Possible sources: (1) a common inference, since "neighbor" in Leviticus meant a fellow Israelite; (2) Psalms that speak of hating God's enemies (Psalm 139:21–22); (3) the Qumran community, whose Community Rule tells members to "love all the sons of light" and "hate all the sons of darkness" (Community Rule 1:9–10). Hebrew "hate" can mean "love less" or "not choose" (Malachi 1:2–3). It is a misreading to say Judaism taught hatred: the Law commands help for an enemy's ox (Exodus 23:4–5), and Proverbs says, "If someone who hates you is hungry, feed him bread" (Proverbs 25:21).
r: Leviticus 19:18; Leviticus 19:34; Psalm 139:21–22; Exodus 23:4–5; Proverbs 25:21; Luke 10:29–37

a: keep loving your enemies
p: Jesus' most famous command. The present tense means an ongoing practice. Later copies add more words.
b: The command has roots in the Law and wisdom (Exodus 23:4–5; Proverbs 25:21–22), but Jesus states it as a rule without limits. "Enemies" for Matthew's hearers included Romans, informers and the persecutors named next. The early church kept this saying at the center: the Didache's first chapter quotes it (Didache 1:3); Jesus prays for his executioners in Luke 23:34, and Stephen for his (Acts 7:60). Paul repeats it in Romans 12:14–21. Byzantine manuscripts add "bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you," from Luke 6:27–28; see the variant.
r: Luke 6:27–28; Luke 6:35; Luke 23:34; Acts 7:60; Romans 12:14–21; Proverbs 25:21–22

a: he lets his sun come up over bad people and good people alike
p: God gives sun and rain to everyone. A Roman philosopher made the same point about the gods.
b: In a farming world, sun and rain were life. God gives them to all without checking who deserves them, so his children should love the same way. To become "sons" is to be like the Father (5:9). The Roman philosopher Seneca, writing in the AD 60s, made a similar argument: if you imitate the gods, do good even to the ungrateful, "for the sun rises also on the wicked" (On Benefits 4.26). Rabbinic teaching also observed that God sends rain on the righteous and the wicked (Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a). The idea was shared; Jesus uses it to ground love for enemies.

a: the tax collectors
p: Local men who bought the right to collect tolls and taxes, often seen as greedy and as working for foreigners.
b: Telōnai were mostly toll and customs collectors. In Galilee they worked for Herod Antipas; in Judea, for Rome's system. Contractors bid for the right to collect and kept what they took above the agreed sum, so many grew rich at others' expense. Jewish writings group them with robbers (Mishnah Nedarim 3:4). Jesus names them as a picture of ordinary moral standards: even they love their friends. Yet he ate with them (9:10–11), and Matthew, called from a tax booth (9:9), was one.

a: if you say hello only to your brothers
p: A greeting was a blessing of peace. Withholding it from outsiders drew a line around one's own group.
b: To greet someone was to wish them peace (shalom) and to recognize them; refusing a greeting shut them out. Jesus' disciples are to greet outsiders too. "The Gentiles" (ethnikoi) were the non-Jewish peoples, in Matthew's Jewish idiom the example of people without God's Law (6:7, 32; 18:17). Byzantine manuscripts read "friends" and "tax collectors" here; see the variants.

a: So you are to be perfect
p: Teleios means complete or whole. It echoes "Be whole with the LORD your God" and "You will be holy."
b: Teleios means complete, mature, whole, having reached its goal. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Deuteronomy 18:13, "Be whole with the LORD your God," and the verse echoes Leviticus 19:2, "You will be holy, because I am holy." Here it sums up the love just described: love that leaves no one out, as God's love does. Luke's parallel reads "Be merciful, as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36). Matthew uses teleios again only in 19:21. Christian traditions have read the verse very differently: as a goal reachable in this life, as a call to all to grow in holiness, or as a standard that drives us to grace. See the card on this page.

a: put your righteousness on show
p: Giving, prayer and fasting were the three great works of Jewish devotion. Jesus treats each the same way.
b: "Righteousness" here means the practice of devotion. Tobit names the same three: "Prayer joined with truth is good, and so are alms joined with doing what is right" (Tobit 12:8, in the longer Greek form of Codex Sinaiticus), and in the shorter Greek form (Vaticanus) the verse reads "prayer with fasting." Jesus does not question the practices; he assumes his followers will do them ("whenever you give," "when you pray," "when you fast"). He questions the audience. Each section follows one pattern: do not do it like the hypocrites, who already have their reward; do it in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will repay you. Later copies read "alms" for "righteousness" here; see the variant.

a: do not have a trumpet blown ahead of you
p: No source says givers literally blew trumpets. It is probably a picture of showing off.
b: No ancient source describes anyone sounding a trumpet when giving to the poor. Suggestions: (1) a picture, like our "blowing your own horn"; (2) the thirteen trumpet-shaped collection chests in the Temple (Mishnah Shekalim 6:5), into which coins rattled loudly; (3) public fast days, when trumpets were blown and donors' gifts were announced. Most scholars take it as a vivid exaggeration. Giving to the poor was a central duty in Judaism, and Jewish teachers also praised secret giving: the Temple had a "chamber of secret gifts," where the devout left gifts and the poor took them without either knowing the other (Mishnah Shekalim 5:6).

a: the hypocrites
p: Hypokritēs was the Greek word for a stage actor, someone playing a part behind a mask.
b: In Greek the hypokritēs was an actor, a performer who played a role for an audience. Jesus uses the image literally here: they perform their devotion "so that people will praise them." Matthew uses the word thirteen times, most often for scribes and Pharisees (15:7; 23:13–29). It does not mean all Pharisees, or all Jews; it names a danger for any religious person, and Matthew's Jesus warns his own disciples against it in these verses.

a: they are already paid in full
p: The verb was used on receipts: "received in full." They got what they wanted, praise, and that is all.
b: Apechousin appears on business receipts in Greek papyri from Egypt with the sense "has received payment in full." The hypocrites wanted human praise, got it, and can expect nothing more. The same line returns in 6:5 and 6:16 like a refrain.
orig: ἀπέχουσιν τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν (apechousin ton misthon autōn)

a: keep your left hand from knowing what your right hand does
p: A picture of giving so quietly that even you hardly notice. It is not a ban on keeping records.
b: The saying is a vivid picture: give so quietly that one hand does not know what the other is doing, which means not keeping score even in your own mind. It does not forbid organized giving. The early church took up collections openly (Acts 4:34–37; 1 Corinthians 16:1–2). The issue is the giver's aim.

a: will repay you
p: Jesus speaks plainly of reward from the Father. Traditions differ on how reward fits with grace.
b: Jesus says the Father "will repay" those who give, pray and fast in secret (6:4, 6, 18), and he speaks of reward in heaven (5:12; 6:20). Both sides quote Augustine, that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts (Letter 194.19; Catechism 2006). Catholic teaching holds that God's grace makes good works truly meritorious, so that the reward is both gift and due (Catechism 2006–2011). Lutheran and Reformed teaching says rewards are free gifts of grace, never merited (Augsburg Confession, article 20; Calvin, Institutes 3.18). Jewish teaching also held both: Antigonus of Sokho taught, "Do not be like slaves who serve their master in order to receive a reward" (Mishnah Avot 1:3), while the rabbis spoke freely of reward in the world to come. Later copies add "openly" (KJV); see the variant.

a: fond of standing up to pray
p: Jews usually stood to pray, at set times of day. Jesus objects to choosing the most public place.
b: Standing was the normal posture for prayer (1 Samuel 1:26; Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13). The central Jewish prayer, the Eighteen Benedictions, is still called the Amidah, "the Standing." Devout Jews prayed at fixed hours, morning, afternoon and evening, wherever they were (Daniel 6:10; Acts 3:1). The Mishnah says that once a man begins his prayer he should not stop, even if a king greets him (Mishnah Berakhot 5:1), so a man whose hour came while he stood at a busy corner could look very devout. Jesus does not forbid public prayer; he warns against using it to be seen.

a: go into the storeroom of your house and close the door behind you
p: The tameion was the inner storeroom, often the only room with a door. The words echo Isaiah 26:20 and Elisha.
b: In a village house the tameion was the storeroom, usually windowless and the only room with a lockable door. The KJV's "closet" meant a small private room. The phrasing recalls the Greek of Isaiah 26:20, "enter your rooms, shut your door," and Elisha, who "closed the door, with only the two of them inside, and he prayed to the LORD" (2 Kings 4:33). The point is not that prayer must be done alone (Jesus teaches "Our Father" in the plural, 6:9), but that it must be done for God, not for an audience.

a: do not chatter on like the Gentiles
p: The rare verb battalogeō means to babble. Pagan prayers often piled up names and titles to get a god's attention.
b: Battalogeō appears almost nowhere in Greek before Matthew; it seems to imitate meaningless speech, like our "blah-blah." Greek and Roman prayers often listed every name and title of a god, to be sure of reaching the right one, and magical texts repeated strings of sounds. The prophets of Baal cried out "from morning until noon" (1 Kings 18:26). Jesus does not forbid long or repeated prayer (26:44; Luke 18:1); he forbids thinking that words work on God like a spell. Ecclesiastes 5:2 had already said, "God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few."

a: Our Father, who is in heaven
p: Jews prayed to God as Father before Jesus. What is new is how central the name becomes for Jesus' disciples.
b: The Hebrew Bible calls God the Father of Israel (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8), and Jewish prayers address him as "Our Father, our King" (Avinu Malkenu). Jesus himself prayed using the Aramaic Abba, "Father" (Mark 14:36), and the early church kept that word (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Joachim Jeremias argued that abba was a family word that no Jew before Jesus used to address God in prayer, though he himself warned against equating it with "Daddy." James Barr ("Abba Isn't Daddy," 1988) and others showed that adults used it too and that it means simply "Father." "Our" makes this a prayer of a community. Luke's shorter form begins simply "Father" (Luke 11:2–4).
orig: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς (Pater hēmōn ho en tois ouranois)
r: Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Mark 14:36; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6; Luke 11:2–4

a: may your name be honored as holy
t: Hallowed be your name: the Kaddish
p: The first two requests closely match the Kaddish, an ancient Jewish prayer: may God's name be holy and his kingdom come.
b: "Hallowed" (KJV) means "treated as holy." God's name stands for God himself as he has made himself known. In Ezekiel 36:23 God says he will show the holiness of his great name by gathering and cleansing his people, so the request asks God to act, not only that people would speak reverently. The Jewish prayer called the Kaddish begins, "Exalted and hallowed be his great name in the world he created by his will, and may he establish his kingdom in your lifetime." Its present wording is later than Jesus, but most scholars think its core is old, and the likeness to 6:9–10 is close. Jesus' prayer is a Jewish prayer.
orig: ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου (hagiasthētō to onoma sou)

a: as in heaven, so also on earth
p: The phrase may finish all three requests: God's name, kingdom and will, on earth as they already are in heaven.
b: The Greek order is "as in heaven, also on earth." Grammatically it can go with the last request only or with all three: that God's name be hallowed, his kingdom come and his will be done on earth as in heaven (Origen read it so). The kingdom is both future, the hope of the end (8:11; 26:29), and already breaking in through Jesus (12:28). Jesus prays the same words about God's will in Gethsemane: "may your will be done" (26:42).

a: our bread for the coming day
p: No one knows exactly what epiousios means. "Daily" is the traditional guess; "for the coming day" is another.
b: Epiousios appears nowhere else in Greek except this prayer (and Luke 11:3); Origen thought the Gospel writers coined it. Main proposals: (1) "for the coming day," from hē epiousa, "the next day": in the morning, today's bread; in the evening, tomorrow's. Jerome says the Gospel of the Hebrews had Aramaic mahar, "tomorrow." (2) "needed for existence," from ousia, "being." (3) "daily," the Old Latin cotidianum, which entered English through the liturgy. (4) "supersubstantial," Jerome's Vulgate word in Matthew, which many church fathers read as the bread of the Eucharist or of the age to come. All fit the memory of manna, given one day at a time (Exodus 16:4). The Plain takes (1) and keeps "today."
orig: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον (ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion)

a: forgive us the debts we owe
p: In Aramaic a "debt" was a common word for sin. Luke says "sins"; many churches say "trespasses."
b: Jesus' Aramaic word hoba meant both a money debt and a sin owed to God, so Matthew's Greek says "debts" and "those who owe us." Luke has "forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who owes us" (Luke 11:4). "Trespasses," used by many English-speaking churches, comes from Tyndale's Bible and the Book of Common Prayer and matches the word in 6:14–15. The past tense, "have forgiven," means that the one praying has already let go of others' debts; later copies have the present "forgive"; see the variant. Jesus' parable in 18:23–35 explains the petition.

a: do not bring us into testing
p: Peirasmos means test, trial or temptation. James says God tempts no one to evil. What is being asked?
b: Peirasmos can be a test of loyalty, a time of trial, or a temptation to sin. The same root is used of Jesus' testing by the devil (4:1) and of Gethsemane, "pray that you do not come into testing" (26:41). James says God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), so the request means: do not let us be put to a test we cannot stand, or do not let us give in. Some read it of the great trial before the end (Revelation 3:10). In recent years the Catholic bishops of France (2017) and Italy (2018) changed their wording to "do not let us enter into temptation" and "do not abandon us to temptation," and Pope Francis supported the change, saying that a father does not lead his child into temptation.
orig: μὴ εἰσενέγκῃς ἡμᾶς εἰς πειρασμόν (mē eisenenkēs hēmas eis peirasmon)

a: rescue us from the evil one
t: From evil, or from the evil one?
p: The Greek can mean "evil" or "the evil one," that is, the devil. Eastern churches have usually read the second.
b: Apo tou ponērou could be neuter ("from evil") or masculine ("from the evil one"). Greek church writers, Chrysostom among them, mostly read "the evil one"; Latin writers such as Augustine often read "evil," and the traditional English prayer follows them. Matthew uses ho ponēros of the devil in 13:19 and 13:38, and the testing of 4:1–11 was by the devil, so "the evil one" fits Matthew. The prayer ends here in the oldest manuscripts; the familiar ending "For yours is the kingdom ..." is a later addition; see the variant.

a: If you forgive people their wrongs
p: Jesus comments on only one request of the prayer: forgiveness. Jewish wisdom taught the same link.
b: Of all the requests, Jesus explains only this one, which shows its weight. Paraptōma, "false step, wrong," is the word behind "trespasses." Sirach, about 180 BC, says, "Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be forgiven when you pray" (Sirach 28:2). Mark has the saying in another setting (Mark 11:25), and the parable of the unforgiving slave makes it a story (18:23–35). Traditions differ on how this condition fits with forgiveness as a free gift; see the card on this page.

a: When you fast
p: Jews fasted on the Day of Atonement and in times of crisis. Devout Pharisees fasted twice a week.
b: The Law required one fast, on the Day of Atonement ("humble yourselves," Leviticus 16:29). Other fasts marked disasters and mourning (Zechariah 8:19; Esther 4:3). The Pharisee in Luke's parable fasts "twice a week" (Luke 18:12), and the Didache tells Christians not to fast with "the hypocrites" on Monday and Thursday but on Wednesday and Friday (Didache 8:1). On public fast days people did not wash or anoint themselves, and wore sackcloth and ashes (Mishnah Taanit 1:6). Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (9:15).

a: They make their faces hard to recognize, so that people will recognize that they are fasting
t: Hiding the face to be seen
p: Jesus plays on two Greek verbs: they make their faces disappear so that they will appear as fasters.
b: Aphanizousin means "they make invisible, disfigure," from a- "not" and phainō "appear"; phanōsin means "they may appear." The Greek reads like a pun: they un-show their faces so as to show off. They left their faces unwashed, smeared with ashes or covered, to look miserable. The Plain keeps the play with "recognize."

a: rub oil into your hair and wash your face
p: Oiling the hair and washing were everyday grooming, and signs of gladness. Fast so no one can tell.
b: In a dry climate, people rubbed olive oil into the hair and skin as daily care and especially for a happy occasion: Naomi tells Ruth to "bathe, rub on scented oil" (Ruth 3:3), and the Psalm speaks of oil making faces glow (Psalm 104:15). Mourners did not anoint themselves (2 Samuel 14:2). David washed and anointed himself when his fasting ended (2 Samuel 12:20). Jesus tells his hearers to look like people on an ordinary day, or even a festive one.

a: moths and rust eat them away
p: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing and grain, which moths and vermin could ruin. Thieves dug through mud walls.
b: In the ancient world wealth was kept in clothing, grain, and coins hidden in the house. Moths ate fine cloth; brōsis, literally "eating," may mean rust on metal, or rot and vermin in stored goods. Burglars "dig through" (diorussō) the mud-brick walls of a house, as Job says: "In the dark one digs through into houses" (Job 24:16). James uses the same images against the rich (James 5:2–3).

a: pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven
p: "Treasure in heaven" was a Jewish way of speaking of good deeds, especially giving, that God remembers.
b: Jewish writers spoke of storing up treasure with God by giving to the poor: "Giving alms is better than storing up gold" (Tobit 12:8), and Sirach says to lay up treasure by the commands of the Most High (Sirach 29:11). Jesus tells the rich young man to sell what he has and give to the poor, "You will have treasure in heaven" (19:21). Treasure in heaven is not a bank account of merit but a life spent on what God values.

a: If your eye is sound
t: A sound eye and an evil eye
p: "Sound" also means generous, and an "evil eye" was a Jewish idiom for stinginess. The saying is about money.
b: Many ancients thought the eye sent light out from the body, like a lamp. But the words also carry a moral sense. Haplous means "single, whole, sound," and its noun means "generosity" (Romans 12:8; 2 Corinthians 8:2). An "evil eye" in Hebrew idiom is a grudging, stingy eye: the Law warns against letting "your eye be evil toward your needy brother" (Deuteronomy 15:9, in the Hebrew), and Proverbs speaks of "a man with a grudging eye" (Proverbs 23:6; 28:22). Jesus uses the idiom again in 20:15. Between sayings about treasure (6:19–21) and serving money (6:24), the point is clear: a generous person is full of light, a greedy one full of darkness.

a: be a slave both to God and to wealth
p: Mammon is Aramaic for wealth or property. Jesus pictures it as a master that wants a slave's whole loyalty.
b: The Greek mamōnas borrows Aramaic mamona, "wealth, property," probably from a root meaning "that in which one trusts." The KJV kept the word as "mammon," and later writers made it a name, almost a false god. The verb douleuō is "to serve as a slave": a slave belonged wholly to one owner, so two owners cannot both have him. "Hate" and "love" here mean "reject" and "choose," as in Hebrew idiom. Luke has the saying after the parable of the shrewd manager (Luke 16:13).

a: stop worrying about your life
p: Merimnaō means to be anxious, pulled in different directions. It appears six times in 6:25–34.
b: The verb merimnaō, "to be anxious, preoccupied," runs through this section (6:25, 27, 28, 31, 34 twice). Jesus does not forbid work or planning (birds still search for food, and the next parable praises a sensible builder, 7:24). He forbids the anxious grasping that comes from not trusting the Father. Psychē is "life" here, the life of the body that needs food, not the "soul" in a later sense. Luke's parallel follows the parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–31).
orig: μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τῇ ψυχῇ ὑμῶν (mē merimnate tē psychē hymōn)

a: your heavenly Father feeds them
p: The Psalms and Job praise God for feeding the young ravens. Luke's version names ravens.
b: "He gives the beasts their food, / and the raven's chicks what they cry out for" (Psalm 147:9). God asks Job, "Who has the raven's meal ready / when its chicks call to God for help?" (Job 38:41). Luke says "consider the ravens" (Luke 12:24), birds the Law counted unclean. The argument runs from lesser to greater, a common Jewish form (qal wa-homer): if God feeds birds, how much more his children (compare 10:29–31).

a: one cubit
p: A cubit was about 18 inches. The word for "life" can also mean height, so some versions speak of height.
b: A cubit (pēchys) was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 45 centimeters. Hēlikia can mean "length of life, age" or "stature, height" (Luke 19:3). The KJV took it as height: "which of you ... can add one cubit unto his stature?" Most modern scholars take it as lifespan, measured in a picture of length, as Psalm 39:5 speaks of days "a handbreadth" long. Adding a foot and a half to one's height would be a huge change, while the point is that worry cannot add even a little to life.
orig: ἐπὶ τὴν ἡλικίαν αὐτοῦ πῆχυν ἕνα (epi tēn hēlikian autou pēchyn hena)

a: the lilies out in the fields
p: The "lilies" were probably wildflowers in general, such as the red anemones that cover Galilee's hills in spring.
b: Krinon can mean a lily but was used loosely of showy wildflowers. Suggestions include the crown anemone, the poppy, the crocus and the Madonna lily. In spring the hills around the Sea of Galilee are covered with red, purple and white flowers for a few weeks, then dry up and are cut for fuel (6:30). "Labor" and "spin" were the work of men in the fields and women at home: the flowers do neither, yet are clothed.

a: Solomon with all his glory
p: Solomon was Israel's model of wealth and splendor; the queen of Sheba was left breathless.
b: When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon's court and "how they were dressed," "it left her breathless" (1 Kings 10:5). Solomon stood in Jewish memory for wisdom, wealth and display (1 Kings 10:14–29). Jesus says a single wildflower is dressed better. Matthew's Gospel later names "something greater than Solomon" in Jesus himself (12:42).

a: you people with so little faith
p: Oligopistos is a word Matthew uses for disciples who trust Jesus, but not enough.
b: Oligopistoi, "you of little faith," is almost a nickname in Matthew (8:26; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20). It is said to disciples, not outsiders: they believe, but their trust fails under pressure. The grass of the field burned in the oven was dried grass and weeds used as fuel for the small clay ovens where bread was baked. Isaiah used the same picture for human frailty: "All flesh is grass" (Isaiah 40:6–8).

a: The Gentiles go hunting for all these things
p: Matthew, writing for Jewish believers, uses "the Gentiles" as shorthand for people who do not know God.
b: Here and in 5:47 and 6:7, "the Gentiles" means people outside Israel's covenant, who (in Jewish eyes) did not know the true God. The usage shows that Matthew's first readers thought of themselves as Jews. The same Gospel ends by sending the disciples to "all the nations" (28:19), and Gentiles like the magi and the centurion appear as models of faith (2:1–12; 8:10). The contrast is about trust in the Father, not about ethnic worth.

a: Seek God's kingdom and his righteousness before anything else
p: God's kingdom and "his righteousness": the right life God asks for, or God's own saving justice?
b: "His righteousness" can mean (1) the righteousness God requires of his people, as elsewhere in the sermon (5:20; 6:1), or (2) God's own justice that he brings when his kingdom comes, as in Isaiah 51:5–8 and Paul (Romans 1:17). Many interpreters read both: seek God's rule and the right life that goes with it. The promise is not wealth but that the Father will provide what is needed (6:32). The oldest manuscripts lack "God's" and simply say "the kingdom"; see the variant. Origen and Clement cite a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels: "Ask for the great things, and the small things will be added to you."

a: Today's trouble is enough for today
p: A proverb-like ending. Proverbs and Ben Sira gave similar advice.
b: "Don't brag about tomorrow, / since you cannot know what a day will give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1). The Babylonian Talmud quotes Ben Sira: "Do not worry about tomorrow's trouble, for you do not know what a day will bring" (Sanhedrin 100b). Kakia here means trouble or hardship, not moral evil. The verse closes the section with a dry, almost humorous realism: each day brings enough trouble without borrowing tomorrow's.

a: Do not judge, so that you are not judged
t: "Do not judge": what it does not mean
p: A common misreading takes this as a ban on all moral judgment. The same chapter requires telling good from bad.
b: Krinō means to judge, to condemn, or to decide. Jesus is not forbidding all discernment: in the same chapter he tells his hearers to tell holy from unholy (7:6), to recognize false prophets by their fruit (7:15–20), and in 18:15–17 to correct a sinning brother. What he forbids is condemning others, setting oneself up as their judge while ignoring one's own faults (7:3–5). The passive "are not judged" points to God's judgment. Hillel said, "Do not judge your fellow until you have come to his place" (Mishnah Avot 2:4). Paul makes the same point (Romans 2:1; 14:4, 10).

a: The measure you use
p: "Measure for measure" was a known Jewish principle of divine justice.
b: The Mishnah states it in almost the same words: "With the measure a person uses to measure, they measure to him" (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). A grain seller's measure could be honest or cheating, heaped up or scraped short (Luke 6:38). God, Jesus says, will judge us by the standard we apply to others. Mark uses the saying of how one hears the word (Mark 4:24).

a: the splinter in your brother's eye
p: A carpenter's joke: a tiny wood chip in one eye, a roof beam in the other. Rabbis used the same picture.
b: Karphos is a chip of wood or straw; dokos a roof beam. The picture is deliberately absurd and comes naturally from a builder's world (13:55). A close parallel appears in the Babylonian Talmud: when someone says, "Take the splinter from between your teeth," the answer is, "Take the beam from between your eyes" (Arakhin 16b). The saying may have been a proverb that Jesus and the rabbis both used.
orig: τὸ κάρφος ... τὴν δοκόν (to karphos ... tēn dokon)

a: Do not give what is holy to the dogs
p: A puzzling saying. The early church applied it to the Lord's Supper; others to preaching or correction.
b: Dogs (scavengers, not pets) and pigs were unclean animals, and both were used as insults for outsiders and the godless (15:26; 2 Peter 2:22; Proverbs 26:11). "What is holy" is singular in Greek, "the holy thing," and may be the meat of sacrifices, which only priests could eat (Exodus 29:33; Leviticus 22:10). Readings: (1) the Didache: "Let no one eat or drink of your Eucharist except those baptized ... for the Lord said, 'Do not give what is holy to the dogs'" (Didache 9:5); (2) do not keep pressing the gospel or correction on people who scorn it (10:14; Proverbs 9:7–8); (3) a balance to 7:1: not judging does not mean having no sense. A guess from the Aramaic ("holy thing" qudsha may be a misreading of qedasha, "ring") links it to Proverbs 11:22, "A gold ring in a pig's snout."

a: Keep asking
t: Keep asking, keep looking, keep knocking
p: The Greek present imperatives suggest continuing action. Seeking God is a theme of the prophets.
b: The commands are in the Greek present tense, which often means ongoing action, and Luke sets them after the parable of the friend who keeps knocking at midnight (Luke 11:5–13). "Seek" and "find" echo God's promise: "You will look for me and you will find me, because you will search for me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13), and "Look for the LORD while he lets himself be found" (Isaiah 55:6). The passives ("it will be given," "it will be opened") again point to God. The promise is not that any wish will be granted but that the Father gives good things (7:11).

a: a stone when the boy asks for bread
t: Bread and stones, fish and snakes
p: A round flat loaf could look like a stone; a fish without scales could look like a snake.
b: Galilean bread was baked in round flat loaves that could look like the stones on a hillside (compare the testing in 4:3). Some fish in the Sea of Galilee, such as the catfish, have no scales and could look like a snake; the Law forbade eating them (Leviticus 11:10). Luke adds an egg and a scorpion (Luke 11:11–12). No father would trick a hungry son like that.

a: You are evil
p: Jesus speaks of his hearers as evil, yet able to do good. Luke ends with the gift of the Holy Spirit.
b: Jesus says this in passing, as a plain fact about human beings compared with God; it is not an insult to one group. Christian teachers have used the line in discussions of human sinfulness (Augustine; the Reformers), while noting that Jesus says evil people still know how to give good gifts. The argument is from lesser to greater: if flawed parents give good things, how much more the Father. Luke's version says the Father will give "the Holy Spirit" (Luke 11:13).

a: whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them
p: The "Golden Rule" is found in many forms. Hillel and Tobit gave the negative form: do not do what you hate.
b: Tobit 4:15 says, "Do not do to anyone what you hate." The Talmud tells of a Gentile who asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot; Hillel answered, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it" (Shabbat 31a). Confucius gave a negative form (Analects 15.24), and Greek writers had others. Jesus' positive form asks more: not only avoiding harm but doing the good you would want. "That is the Law and the Prophets" closes the main body of the sermon begun at 5:17, and anticipates 22:40.

a: Go in by the narrow gate
p: The picture of two ways, one to life and one to death, runs from Deuteronomy to the Didache.
b: Moses set before Israel "life and what is good, death and what is bad" (Deuteronomy 30:15), and Jeremiah 21:8 speaks of "the way of life and the way of death." Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. The early Christian Didache opens, "There are two ways, one of life and one of death" (Didache 1:1). Jesus adds the gate and the crowd: the easy road is popular. Luke has "Struggle to get in through the narrow door" (Luke 13:24). "Ruin" (apōleia) is destruction, the opposite of "life."
r: Deuteronomy 30:15; Deuteronomy 30:19; Jeremiah 21:8; Psalm 1:6; Luke 13:23–24; 2 Peter 2:1–3

a: how cramped the road leading to life
p: Tethlimmenē means squeezed or hard pressed. Its noun is thlipsis, the word for persecution and tribulation.
b: The participle tethlimmenē means "pressed, crowded, hemmed in." Its noun thlipsis is the word for trouble and persecution in 13:21 and 24:9, 21, 29. So the narrow road is not only hard to find but a way of hardship, as the Beatitudes warned (5:10–12). "Life" here is the life of the age to come (19:16–17; 25:46). The oldest copies differ between "How narrow" and "For narrow"; see the variant.

a: Be on your guard against false prophets
p: The Law gave tests for false prophets. Matthew's church faced prophets inside its own fold.
b: The Law warned against prophets who lead the people to other gods even if their signs come true (Deuteronomy 13:1–3), and against one who speaks a word in God's name "that I did not command him" (Deuteronomy 18:20). Ezekiel called Israel's corrupt leaders wolves tearing their prey (Ezekiel 22:27). Jesus warns that false prophets will appear among his followers, looking like sheep (24:11, 24). The early Didache gives practical tests: a prophet who stays more than two days or asks for money is false (Didache 11). The test here is fruit: conduct over time.

a: Any tree that fails to produce good fruit is being cut down and thrown into a fire
p: Jesus repeats John the Baptist's warning in 3:10, in the same Greek except for one small word.
b: The Greek of this verse is John the Baptist's warning in 3:10 without its connecting word oun, "so," and the English here matches 3:10. The Greek "into fire" has no article; English needs "the." Matthew lets Jesus and John speak with one voice (compare 3:2 and 4:17). Fruit is a common Bible picture for the deeds that show a person's real nature (3:8; 12:33–35; 21:43; Galatians 5:22). Burning unfruitful trees was ordinary farm practice, and the prophets used it for judgment (Isaiah 10:33–34; Jeremiah 11:16).

a: Not all who call me 'Lord, Lord'
p: Calling Jesus "Lord" is not enough. The test is doing the Father's will.
b: Kyrie could be a polite "sir," but here, doubled and in a scene of final judgment, it is the confession of the church. Jesus speaks of himself as the one people will address on that day, and of God as "my Father." The stress on doing the Father's will runs through Matthew (12:50; 21:28–32; 25:31–46). Traditions read the verse in light of their teaching on faith and works: some see true faith proved by obedience, others see the need to cooperate with grace, and all agree it rules out empty words. Luke has "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I say?" (Luke 6:46).

a: When that day comes
p: "That day" is the day of judgment, the prophets' "day of the LORD." Miracles alone do not prove anything.
b: The prophets spoke of "that day" when God judges and saves (Isaiah 2:11–12; Zephaniah 1:14–15; Malachi 3:17–18). In Matthew Jesus is the judge on that day (16:27; 25:31). The speakers claim prophecy, exorcism and miracles "by your name," the very things the disciples will do (10:1, 8). Yet Jesus does not deny their deeds; he denies knowing them. The Law had said signs and wonders can come from false prophets (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

a: Leave me, you who practice lawlessness!
p: The words echo Psalm 6:8 in its Greek form. "Lawlessness" is one of Matthew's key words.
b: The Psalm says, "Leave me, every one of you who does wrong!" (Psalm 6:8); the Greek Psalm has the same words Matthew uses, "workers of lawlessness." Anomia, "lawlessness," means disregard for God's law; Matthew uses it for the hypocrites (23:28), for the evildoers removed from the kingdom (13:41), and for the last days (24:12). For a Gospel that insists the Law stands (5:17–19), "lawlessness" is the root sin. "I never knew you" means "I never had any relationship with you" (compare 25:12).
orig: οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν (hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian)

a: built his house on bedrock
p: "The rock" (petra) is the same word Jesus uses in 16:18. Wise and foolish builders recall Proverbs.
b: Petra is bedrock, the solid rock under the soil. Jesus will use the same word in "on this rock I will build my church" (16:18). The sensible (phronimos) and foolish (mōros) builders are a pair like the sensible and foolish bridesmaids of 25:1–13, and like the wise and the fool of Proverbs. Isaiah speaks of a tested cornerstone and a storm that sweeps away a refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:16–17), and Ezekiel of a whitewashed wall that falls in the rain (Ezekiel 13:10–14). In Luke's version the wise man digs deep (Luke 6:47–49).

a: in came the floods
p: In winter rains, dry valleys in the land of Israel can turn into torrents within minutes.
b: The "rivers" (potamoi) are the sudden torrents that rush down dry wadis after a heavy winter storm. A flat sandy wadi floor could look like an easy building site in summer; in winter a flood could wash a house away. Many readers hear the storm as a picture of God's final judgment (compare Isaiah 28:17; Ezekiel 13:11–13), not only the troubles of life.

a: When Jesus finished these words
t: The formula that ends each discourse
p: Matthew closes each of Jesus' five long speeches with almost the same words, as Moses "finished speaking."
b: The phrase "when Jesus finished" ends each of the five great speeches in Matthew (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Many scholars compare the five books of Moses, and the Greek of Deuteronomy, where Moses "had finished speaking all these words" (Deuteronomy 32:45; compare Deuteronomy 31:1). Others count the speeches differently or doubt the comparison. The crowds who listened (5:1; 7:28) show that the sermon was spoken to the disciples but within the hearing of all.

a: not as their scribes did
p: The scribes taught by citing tradition. Jesus taught on his own authority. "Their" scribes shows Matthew's distance from the synagogue.
b: Scribes explained the Law by quoting earlier teachers and Scripture. Jesus' "But I myself tell you" (5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44) carried authority of its own, which Matthew later grounds in the risen Jesus: "I have been given all authority, in heaven and on earth" (28:18). Mark has the same observation at Capernaum (Mark 1:22). Matthew writes "their scribes," as he writes "their synagogues" (4:23; 9:35), which many scholars read as a sign that his community had separated from the synagogue led by other Jews. This was a family quarrel among Jews, not a judgment on a people.
